chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
title: Milwaukee success, then Kirby's five-hundred-dollar draw in Chicago
summary: After a hit in Milwaukee, Kirby demanded a $500 draw from a gangster-run Chicago club and the band was let go after a week.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: But you had Nelson Williams there, didn't you?

No, no, no. This was the first time. Rostelle Reese was the trumpet player. And we go there and we made a big hit, an awful big hit in Milwaukee. And everybody liked us. The boss liked us, and the people liked us. It was really a nice engagement. But he had booked other things, they had booked other bands behind us, you know. I think we stayed there four weeks. And then they brought in Charlie Ventura's band.
So we go to Chicago to work, and we work in a nightclub in Chicago... We followed Red Allen into this club. Kirby with his biggity ideas, even the first night we opened up,

he wanted to make a draw... He wanted to draw some money in Chicago. And he goes to the boss and asks for I think a five hundred dollar draw. The boss looked at him like he was crazy. The first night he comes on the job he wants to draw five hundred dollars. Kirby says, "Well, if I can't get it, if I can't get five hundred dollars tonight, you can get you another band in here. At the end of the week, you get another band." So these was all gangsters we was workin' for. He said, "Get another band." So what?

So we stayed there a week, one week, and he taken us out, taken us out in the street. He goes down... So we're doin' nothin' now. We're layin' around Chicago, and we don't have anything to do. So we're just layin' around, bidin' the time away. Kirby's out trying to dig up something.
